title: Employment Lawyer Cost: Contingency, Hourly and Fee-Shifting (2026)
description: Employment and wrongful termination lawyer costs for employees and employers: contingency vs hourly, fee-shifting, damages caps and EEOC deadlines.
h1: How much does an employment lawyer cost?
summary: Employees with discrimination, wage or wrongful termination claims often hire employment lawyers on contingency or a hybrid fee, because Title VII lets courts award fees to winning employees and the FLSA requires them. Employers usually pay hourly; Clio's 2025 average for employment lawyers is $387 per hour. Deadlines matter: an EEOC charge is generally due within 180 days of the discriminatory act, or 300 days where a state or local agency enforces a similar law.
body:
The answer depends on which side you are on

Employment lawyers price their work very differently for employees and for employers. Employees with claims such as discrimination, retaliation, unpaid wages or wrongful termination often find lawyers who work on contingency or a hybrid arrangement, because federal fee-shifting laws can make the employer pay. Employers almost always pay hourly. Clio's 2025 data puts the average employment and labor lawyer rate at $387 per hour, above the $349 all-lawyer average [1].

For employees: contingency, hourly or hybrid

  • Contingency. The lawyer takes an agreed percentage of any recovery and usually advances case costs. Lawyers accept only cases where provable damages justify the risk.
  • Hourly or flat fee for advice. Reviewing a severance agreement, a non-compete or a final paycheck problem is often billed by the hour or as a flat fee.
  • Hybrid. A reduced hourly rate plus a smaller contingency percentage, used when damages are uncertain.

Example (illustrative, assuming a one-third contingency fee): a $90,000 settlement with $6,000 in case costs. If the fee is calculated on the gross amount: $90,000 × 1/3 = $30,000 fee; you receive $90,000 − $30,000 − $6,000 = $54,000. If costs come off first: ($90,000 − $6,000) × 1/3 = $28,000 fee; you receive $56,000. Ask which method your agreement uses. See the contingency fee calculator.

Example (illustrative): a severance review that takes 3 hours at the $387 employment average costs 3 × $387 = $1,161.

Fee-shifting: when the employer pays your lawyer

  • Title VII (discrimination, harassment, retaliation): the court may award the prevailing party a reasonable attorney's fee, including expert fees [3]. Prevailing employers rarely recover fees: only if the employee's claim was frivolous, unreasonable or without foundation [4].
  • Fair Labor Standards Act (minimum wage, overtime): the court must award a reasonable attorney's fee and costs, paid by the employer, when employees win, and unpaid wages can be doubled through an equal amount of liquidated damages [5]. That mandatory fee is why many lawyers take small wage cases.

Damages caps also shape case economics. Under Title VII and the ADA, combined compensatory and punitive damages are capped at $50,000 for employers with 15 to 100 employees, $100,000 for 101 to 200, $200,000 for 201 to 500 and $300,000 above 500; back pay is not counted toward the cap [6]. State anti-discrimination laws can have different damages rules, which is one reason lawyers often consider state claims too.

Deadlines that decide whether you have a case

Most federal discrimination claims must start with a charge at the EEOC, not a lawsuit:

  • 180 calendar days from the discriminatory act to file a charge, extended to 300 days if a state or local agency enforces a law against the same type of discrimination [2].
  • Age claims: the 300-day extension applies only if a state law and state agency cover age discrimination; a local law alone does not extend it [2].
  • Equal Pay Act: no EEOC charge is needed; you can sue within 2 years, or 3 years for willful violations [2].
  • Federal employees: generally must contact an agency EEO counselor within 45 days [2].
  • After the EEOC: once you receive a right-to-sue notice, a Title VII lawsuit must be filed within 90 days [3].
Missing these deadlines can end a claim no matter how strong it is. If you were fired or demoted and suspect discrimination, talk to a lawyer well before day 180.

Wrongful termination claims

Most U.S. employment is "at will," so being fired unfairly is not by itself illegal. A firing is usually a legal claim only if it was discriminatory, retaliatory (for example, for reporting harassment, wage violations or safety problems), in breach of a written contract, or in violation of a specific state law. That is why a lawyer's first consultation focuses on why you were fired and what documents you have.

What drives the cost of a termination case

  • Arbitration agreements. If you signed one, the case may go to private arbitration instead of court, which changes timing, discovery and costs.
  • Evidence. Emails, performance reviews and witnesses reduce the hours a lawyer must spend building the case.
  • Size of the loss. Lost pay while you look for work is the backbone of most damages; finding a new job quickly lowers both damages and the lawyer's appetite for contingency.
  • Severance on the table. Negotiating a better severance is often faster and cheaper than litigation.

Severance agreements and age claims

If you are 40 or older and the severance asks you to release age-discrimination claims, federal law requires at least 21 days to consider it (45 days in group layoffs) and at least 7 days to revoke after signing [7]. Use that time to have a lawyer review it.

For employers: what you are paying for

Employers pay hourly or by flat fee for policy drafting, handbook updates, employment contracts, worker classification advice and defense of charges and lawsuits. Classification matters: treating an employee as an independent contractor can expose a business to back wages, liquidated damages and the employee's attorney fees under the FLSA [5]. A contract template does not decide classification; how the work is actually controlled does.

Example (illustrative): responding to an EEOC charge with a position statement that takes 15 hours at $387 per hour costs 15 × $387 = $5,805.

Bring this to your first consultation

  • Offer letter, contract, handbook and any arbitration agreement.
  • Termination letter, severance offer and its deadline.
  • Pay stubs and records of hours worked.
  • A timeline with dates of complaints, discipline and the firing.
  • Names of witnesses and copies of relevant emails or texts you lawfully have.

faq.q: Do employment lawyers work on contingency?
faq.a: Many employee-side lawyers do for discrimination, retaliation and wage cases, especially where fee-shifting laws like Title VII and the FLSA apply. They screen cases for provable damages first. Advice-only work such as a severance review is usually hourly or a flat fee.

faq.q: Will I have to pay my employer's lawyer if I lose?
faq.a: Under Title VII, only if a court finds your claim was frivolous, unreasonable or without foundation. Other laws and contracts can have different rules, so ask about fee-shifting in your consultation, especially if you signed an arbitration agreement.

faq.q: How long do I have to file a discrimination claim?
faq.a: Generally 180 calendar days from the discriminatory act to file an EEOC charge, or 300 days in places where a state or local agency enforces a similar law. Equal Pay Act claims go straight to court within 2 years, or 3 if willful.

faq.q: Is it worth paying a lawyer to review my severance agreement?
faq.a: Often, when the agreement releases claims you might have, includes a non-compete, or the amount is significant. If you are 40 or older and asked to release age claims, federal law gives you at least 21 days to consider it and 7 days to revoke after signing.

faq.q: Can I sue for being fired without a reason?
faq.a: Usually not, because most jobs are at will. A firing becomes a legal claim when it was discriminatory, retaliatory, in breach of a contract, or violated a specific law.
